courses.title: 1. Kubernetes architecture & control plane
courses.summary: Master the distributed architecture of Kubernetes (CKA domain: Cluster Architecture & Installation): kube-apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager, kubelet, kube-proxy, and declarative reconciliation.
courses.code:
# Kubernetes core architecture manifest: Namespace isolation, ResourceQuota,
# LimitRange default constraints, and a foundational Pod.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: prod-workloads
  labels:
    environment: production
    app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: declarative-gitops
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: prod-workloads
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "10"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: prod-workloads
spec:
  limits:
    - default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 250m
        memory: 256Mi
      type: Container
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: core-web
  namespace: prod-workloads
  labels:
    app: core-web
    tier: frontend
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.27-alpine
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: http
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 250m
          memory: 256Mi
        limits:
          cpu: 500m
          memory: 512Mi
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-architecture.yaml`: creates the `prod-workloads` namespace, enforces resource quotas and limit ranges, and schedules the `core-web` pod in running state within quota bounds.

lessons.title: The control plane components
paragraphs: The Kubernetes control plane manages the worker nodes and pods across the cluster. It consists of four primary components: kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, and kube-controller-manager. The kube-apiserver is the front door of the control plane; it exposes the Kubernetes HTTP/JSON REST API, performs authentication, authorization, and admission control, and is the only component that interacts directly with etcd.

etcd is a strongly consistent, distributed key-value store (using the Raft consensus algorithm) that holds the authoritative cluster state. The kube-scheduler monitors newly created pods without an assigned node and selects the optimal node based on resource requirements and affinity policies. The kube-controller-manager runs core reconciliation loops (NodeLifecycle, ReplicaSet, Endpoints) that continuously steer the cluster toward the desired state.
lessons.example: Client request -> kube-apiserver (validates) -> etcd (persists state) -> scheduler (assigns node) -> kubelet (starts container).
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to access or modify etcd directly bypasses validation, audit logs, and admission webhooks, corrupting cluster state.

question.prompt: Which component is the only one that directly reads from and writes to etcd?
question.explanation: kube-apiserver is the sole stateless gateway to etcd; all other components interact via the apiserver REST API.

lessons.title: Worker node anatomy
paragraphs: Worker nodes execute containerized workloads. Every worker node runs three fundamental software components: the container runtime, kubelet, and kube-proxy. The container runtime (such as containerd or CRI-O) pulls container images and runs containers, communicating with Kubernetes via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) gRPC protocol.

kubelet is the primary node agent that registers the node with the apiserver, watches for PodSpecs assigned to its node, and ensures the described containers are running and healthy. kube-proxy maintains network rules (using iptables or IPVS) on each node to forward network traffic targeting Service virtual IPs directly to the appropriate backend pod endpoints.
lessons.example: kubelet watches PodSpecs for its node and calls CRI to pull images and start containers.
lessons.pitfall: Confusing kubelet with kube-proxy: kubelet manages container lifecycles on the node, while kube-proxy manages L4 network routing rules.

question.prompt: The node agent responsible for watching PodSpecs and instructing the container runtime is:
question.explanation: kubelet runs on every worker node and interacts with the container runtime via CRI.

lessons.title: Declarative reconciliation loop
paragraphs: Kubernetes is built entirely on declarative design rather than imperative execution. In declarative management, you declare the desired state in YAML or JSON manifests (e.g. 'run exactly 3 replicas of my web app'). Controllers in the control plane continuously execute a reconciliation control loop: observe current state, compare it with desired state, and execute corrective mutations to close the delta.

This control loop makes Kubernetes self-healing. If a worker node crashes or a container is killed, the controller detects that actual replicas (2) are less than desired replicas (3) and automatically schedules a replacement pod on an available healthy node without human intervention.
lessons.example: Desired = 3, Actual = 2 -> Controller schedules 1 new pod -> Desired == Actual.
lessons.pitfall: Treating Kubernetes imperatively with ad-hoc manual docker or kubectl run commands loses the auditability and self-healing guarantees of declarative manifests.

question.prompt: What does a Kubernetes controller do during its reconciliation loop?

options.text: Compiles container binaries from Git repositories
Observes actual state, diffs against desired state, and acts to resolve differences
Executes SQL database migrations on every commit

question.explanation: Controllers continually observe actual state, compare it to desired state recorded in etcd, and reconcile the differences.

lessons.title: Namespaces, Quotas & LimitRanges
paragraphs: Namespaces provide logical virtual clusters within a single physical Kubernetes cluster. They partition resource names, enable multi-team tenancy, and serve as security and authorization boundaries for Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and NetworkPolicies.

To prevent noisy-neighbor syndrome where one team exhausts cluster compute, administrators apply ResourceQuotas (hard limits on total CPU, memory, and object counts per namespace) and LimitRanges (default, minimum, and maximum CPU and memory requirements enforced per container if omitted by developers).
lessons.example: ResourceQuota caps total RAM in `team-a` to 16Gi; LimitRange injects default 250m CPU if not specified.
lessons.pitfall: Creating a ResourceQuota without defining a LimitRange causes pod creation to fail if developers omit explicit resource requests in their manifests.

question.prompt: What happens if a namespace has a ResourceQuota for CPU and a pod is submitted without CPU requests or limits (with no LimitRange)?

options.text: The pod is admitted with unlimited CPU allocation
The apiserver rejects the pod with a validation error
The node automatically sets CPU to 100 millicores

question.explanation: When a quota is placed on compute resources, pods must specify explicit requests/limits or have defaults injected by a LimitRange; otherwise the apiserver rejects admission.

steps: Inspect the cluster control plane status: run `kubectl cluster-info` and `kubectl get nodes -o wide` to observe worker nodes and their container runtime.
Apply the architecture manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-architecture.yaml` to create the namespace, quota, limit range, and pod.
Verify the namespace and resource constraints: run `kubectl get resourcequotas,limitranges -n prod-workloads`.
Inspect the running pod: execute `kubectl describe pod core-web -n prod-workloads` and observe that the LimitRange defaults and explicit resources are active.

challenge.task: Create a multi-tenant namespace with a strict ResourceQuota of 2 pods and verify that attempting to create a third pod is rejected by the admission controller.
acceptance: Namespace and ResourceQuota manifests with hard pod limit of 2
Successful creation of two pods within the namespace
CLI output demonstrating apiserver rejection on attempting to schedule the 3rd pod

questions.prompt: Which component watches for newly created pods without assigned nodes and selects an appropriate node for them?
questions.explanation: kube-scheduler is responsible for assigning unscheduled pods to eligible worker nodes.

questions.prompt: What consensus protocol does etcd use to maintain state consistency across control plane replicas?
questions.explanation: etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm for distributed leader election and log replication.

questions.prompt: Which protocol defines the interface between kubelet and the underlying container runtime?
questions.explanation: CRI defines the gRPC API that kubelet uses to interact with container engines like containerd.

questions.prompt: How does Kubernetes restore a crashed container back to running status?

options.text: A human operator must execute `docker restart` via SSH
kubelet detects container termination and restarts it per the pod restartPolicy
etcd triggers a full cluster reboot

questions.explanation: kubelet monitors running containers and restarts terminated ones according to the restartPolicy (Always, OnFailure, Never).

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a LimitRange in a Kubernetes namespace?

options.text: To set maximum CPU limits for the entire cluster nodes
To specify default, min, and max compute constraints per individual container
To limit the number of external IP addresses assigned by cloud load balancers

questions.explanation: LimitRanges enforce default, min, and max compute allocations for individual containers and pods in a namespace.

courses.title: 2. Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments
courses.summary: Master the Pod lifecycle, multi-container init and sidecar patterns, ReplicaSets, and zero-downtime rolling updates with Deployments (CKAD & CKA: Workloads & Scheduling).
courses.code:
# Production Deployment: ReplicaSet management, zero-downtime rolling updates,
# initContainer database dependency check, and logging sidecar container.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-service
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: api-service
    app.kubernetes.io/component: backend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-service
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: wait-for-dependencies
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo "Checking database readiness..."; sleep 2; echo "Ready!"']
      containers:
        - name: web-api
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              name: http
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: shared-logs
              mountPath: /var/log/nginx
        - name: log-shipper
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -F /var/log/nginx/access.log 2>/dev/null || sleep 3600']
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: shared-logs
              mountPath: /var/log/nginx
      volumes:
        - name: shared-logs
          emptyDir: {}
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-pods-workloads.yaml`: runs the init container, starts 3 replicas each with the web-api container and log-shipper sidecar sharing an emptyDir volume, guaranteeing zero unavailable pods during updates.

lessons.title: The Pod as the atomic scheduling unit
paragraphs: A Pod is the smallest deployable computing unit you can create and manage in Kubernetes. A Pod encapsulates one or more containers that share storage resources (Volumes), an IP address, and network namespaces. Containers within the same Pod communicate with each other via `localhost` and share shared IPC mechanisms.

Pods have distinct phases: Pending (accepted by cluster but not yet running on a node), Running (bound to a node and at least one container is active), Succeeded (all containers terminated cleanly with exit code 0), Failed (at least one container failed with non-zero exit code), and Unknown (state cannot be determined by the apiserver).
lessons.example: Two containers in the same Pod talk to each other over `localhost:8080` without traversing cluster networking.
lessons.pitfall: Deploying independent microservices in a single Pod: Pods should only contain tightly coupled processes that must share lifecycle and network namespace.

question.prompt: How do two containers located inside the exact same Pod communicate with each other over the network?

options.text: Over localhost using standard loopback ports
They cannot communicate over network protocols

question.explanation: Containers within a single Pod share the same network namespace and loopback interface, allowing communication via localhost.

lessons.title: Init containers and sidecar patterns
paragraphs: Init containers run to completion sequentially before any app containers start. If an init container fails with a non-zero exit code, Kubernetes restarts the Pod until the init container succeeds (per restartPolicy). This makes init containers ideal for pre-flight tasks: running database schema migrations, waiting for external services to be reachable, or pulling sensitive keys.

Sidecar containers run concurrently alongside the main application container. Common sidecar patterns include logging agents (shipping local logs from a shared emptyDir volume to Elasticsearch), service mesh proxies (Envoy handling mTLS and observability), and secret synchronizers (fetching tokens from Vault into local memory).
lessons.example: Init container verifies DB is listening on port 5432; once complete, the app container launches.
lessons.pitfall: Putting long-running polling without timeouts in init containers can block the Pod in `Init:0/1` status indefinitely.

question.prompt: When do application containers in a Pod start running in relation to init containers?

options.text: Concurrently in parallel with all init containers
Only after all init containers have executed and terminated successfully

question.explanation: Init containers execute sequentially and each must complete successfully before application containers begin execution.

lessons.title: ReplicaSets and declarative controllers
paragraphs: A ReplicaSet's purpose is to maintain a stable set of replica Pods running at any given time. It uses a label selector (`matchLabels` or `matchExpressions`) to identify which Pods belong to it. If Pods crash or are deleted, the ReplicaSet creates new ones; if extra matching Pods are created manually, the ReplicaSet terminates the excess to match the desired `replicas` count.

Although ReplicaSets guarantee availability, you rarely manage ReplicaSets directly in production. Instead, you declare Deployments, which manage ReplicaSets automatically under the hood to enable rolling updates, rollbacks, and declarative state revisions.
lessons.example: Deployment `api-service` creates ReplicaSet `api-service-6789b5` which manages 3 Pods matching `app: api-service`.
lessons.pitfall: Creating bare Pods without a controller like a Deployment or ReplicaSet means that if the worker node reboots, the Pods will not be rescheduled.

question.prompt: Why should production workloads be managed by Deployments rather than creating standalone Pods?

options.text: Standalone Pods cannot use container images from Docker Hub
Standalone Pods are not rescheduled or replaced if the worker node crashes
Deployments consume 50% less RAM than standalone Pods

question.explanation: Bare Pods lack a managing controller; if their node fails or they are evicted, Kubernetes does not automatically recreate them.

lessons.title: Zero-downtime rolling updates & rollbacks
paragraphs: Deployments support two update strategies: Recreate (kills all existing pods before creating new ones, causing downtime) and RollingUpdate (gradually replaces old pods with new ones). RollingUpdate behavior is configured using two crucial parameters: `maxUnavailable` (maximum number of pods that can be unavailable during the update) and `maxSurge` (maximum number of pods that can be created above the desired replica count).

Setting `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1` guarantees zero downtime: Kubernetes spins up 1 new pod, waits for its readinessProbe to pass, and only then terminates 1 old pod. If an update fails, running `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-service` rolls back to the previous known good ReplicaSet revision instantly.
lessons.example: `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` ensures at least 100% capacity is always serving incoming traffic during deployments.
lessons.pitfall: Setting `maxUnavailable: 100%` causes the Deployment to terminate all existing pods simultaneously, equivalent to a Recreate strategy with full outage.

question.prompt: Which configuration guarantees that capacity never drops below the desired replica count during a rolling update?
question.explanation: With maxUnavailable: 0, no running pods are terminated until new surrogate pods have become ready, preventing capacity drops.

steps: Apply the Deployment manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-pods-workloads.yaml`.
Monitor rollout progression: run `kubectl rollout status deployment/api-service` to observe init container completion and pod readiness.
Trigger a rolling update by updating the container image: run `kubectl set image deployment/api-service web-api=nginx:1.27.2-alpine`.
Inspect rollout history and undo: run `kubectl rollout history deployment/api-service`, then execute `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-service` to restore the previous revision.

challenge.task: Configure a Deployment with 4 replicas that executes a zero-downtime rolling update, verifies new pod readiness, and retains 10 historical revisions.
acceptance: Deployment manifest specifying 4 replicas and revisionHistoryLimit of 10
RollingUpdate strategy configured with maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 25%
Demonstration of `kubectl rollout history` and rollback verification

questions.prompt: What Pod phase indicates that all containers in the Pod have terminated successfully with exit code 0?
questions.explanation: The Succeeded phase means all containers in the Pod have successfully terminated and will not be restarted.

questions.prompt: If an init container fails with exit code 1, what does kubelet do next by default (restartPolicy: Always)?

options.text: Skips the init container and starts the main application containers
Restarts the Pod repeatedly with exponential backoff until the init container succeeds
Deletes the worker node from the cluster

questions.explanation: Kubelet repeatedly restarts the failed init container until it exits with code 0 before proceeding to application containers.

questions.prompt: How does a ReplicaSet know which Pods it is responsible for managing?

options.text: It matches Pods using its label selector (spec.selector.matchLabels)
By the node IP address where the Pod was created

questions.explanation: ReplicaSets identify their target Pods using declarative label selectors.

questions.prompt: What CLI command allows you to view the list of revisions recorded for a Deployment?
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout history` inspects the historical ReplicaSet revisions created during deployment updates.

questions.prompt: What volume type allows two containers in the same Pod to share a temporary directory that exists as long as the Pod is running?
questions.explanation: An emptyDir volume is initially empty and shares storage between containers in the same Pod for the lifespan of that Pod.

courses.title: 3. ConfigMaps, Secrets & Environment Injection
courses.summary: Decouple configuration and sensitive credentials from container images using ConfigMaps, Secrets, volume mounts, and immutability (CKAD: Application Configuration).
courses.code:
# Decoupled configuration: ConfigMap with files and literals, Secret with base64 data,
# and a Deployment injecting them via envFrom and volumeMounts.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
  labels:
    app: backend-worker
spec:
  immutable: true
data:
  ENVIRONMENT: "production"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  app-settings.json: |
    {
      "cacheEnabled": true,
      "poolSize": 20,
      "timeoutMs": 5000
    }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  labels:
    app: backend-worker
type: Opaque
immutable: true
data:
  # Base64 encoded values (echo -n "..." | base64)
  # postgres_user: dbadmin
  DB_USER: ZGJhZG1pbg==
  # postgres_pass: S3cur3P@ssw0rd!
  DB_PASSWORD: UzNjdXIzUEBzc3cwcmQh
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend-worker
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend-worker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          env:
            - name: DB_USER
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-credentials
                  key: DB_USER
            - name: DB_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-credentials
                  key: DB_PASSWORD
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: app-config
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config-volume
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: config-volume
          configMap:
            name: app-config
            items:
              - key: app-settings.json
                path: settings.json
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-config-secrets.yaml`: creates immutable ConfigMap and Secret, mounts `settings.json` at `/etc/app/config/settings.json`, and injects environment variables into worker pods.

lessons.title: Decoupling configuration with ConfigMaps
paragraphs: The Twelve-Factor App methodology mandates strict separation of config from code. Hardcoding configuration values inside container images forces you to rebuild images across development, staging, and production environments.

A ConfigMap stores non-confidential data in key-value pairs. Values can be simple scalar strings or multiline configuration files (such as `nginx.conf`, JSON, or YAML). Pods consume ConfigMaps as environment variables, command-line arguments, or mounted configuration files in a Volume.
lessons.example: Change `LOG_LEVEL` from `debug` to `warn` by updating the ConfigMap without rebuilding the Docker image.
lessons.pitfall: Storing passwords, API tokens, or TLS private keys in ConfigMaps: ConfigMaps are unencrypted plaintext objects; always use Secrets for credentials.

question.prompt: What is the primary benefit of storing configuration in ConfigMaps rather than inside container images?

options.text: It encrypts all configuration using AES-256 automatically
It decouples environment-specific settings from immutable container images
It allows containers to run without requiring a container runtime

question.explanation: ConfigMaps decouple configuration from container images so the same image runs across different environments.

lessons.title: Secrets types and security boundaries
paragraphs: Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive data like passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys. Secret types include `Opaque` (arbitrary user-defined key-value pairs), `kubernetes.io/tls` (TLS certificates and private keys), and `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` (container image registry credentials). Data entries in Secret manifests are Base64 encoded.

Crucially, Base64 encoding is NOT encryption; it is simply reversible data obfuscation. True security requires enabling Encryption at Rest for etcd (`EncryptionConfiguration` with AES-CBC or KMS providers) and implementing strict RBAC policies restricting who can read Secrets.
lessons.example: Encode a secret value: `echo -n 'my-password' | base64` -> `bXktcGFzc3dvcmQ=`.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming Base64 encoding provides confidentiality: anyone with `kubectl get secret -o yaml` can decode it instantly with `base64 -d`.

question.prompt: Why is Base64 encoding in Kubernetes Secret YAML files NOT considered security encryption?

options.text: Because Base64 is a reversible encoding scheme requiring no secret key to decode
Because Base64 can only store numbers
Because Base64 is only supported on Linux

question.explanation: Base64 is a standard encoding format that anyone can decode without a cryptographic key.

lessons.title: Environment variables vs volume mounts
paragraphs: Kubernetes provides two mechanisms to expose ConfigMaps and Secrets to containers: environment variables (`env` / `envFrom`) and Volume mounts (`volumeMounts`). Environment variables are static: when a ConfigMap or Secret is updated in the cluster, already-running processes do NOT receive the updated values until the Pod is restarted.

In contrast, mounting a ConfigMap or Secret as a volume mounts files into the container filesystem. Kubelet periodically reconciles mounted volumes (via symlinks to projected files); when the ConfigMap is modified, the mounted files update atomically inside the running container without requiring a Pod restart.
lessons.example: A mounted `/etc/app/config/settings.json` updates automatically when the ConfigMap changes; `env` variables do not.
lessons.pitfall: Using `subPath` when mounting a single file from a ConfigMap: files mounted using `subPath` do NOT receive automatic updates when the ConfigMap changes.

question.prompt: What happens to a running container's environment variables when the referenced ConfigMap is modified?

options.text: Environment variables update immediately within 1 millisecond
Environment variables do not update until the Pod is restarted or redeployed
The container crashes immediately with a SIGTERM

question.explanation: Environment variables are injected at process startup; changes to the ConfigMap do not affect existing running processes until restarted.

lessons.title: Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
paragraphs: Starting in Kubernetes 1.21, ConfigMaps and Secrets can be marked with `immutable: true`. Once marked immutable, any attempt to modify their `data` or `binaryData` is rejected by the kube-apiserver. To update configuration, teams create a new ConfigMap with a unique name (e.g. `app-config-v2`) and update the Deployment manifest.

Immutability offers two immense benefits: protection against accidental misconfigurations corrupting production workloads, and significant performance gains. Because kubelet knows the object cannot change, it closes all watch streams to the kube-apiserver, dramatically reducing cluster control plane load.
lessons.example: `immutable: true` prevents inadvertent edits and triggers safe rolling deployments via new ConfigMap names.
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to edit an immutable ConfigMap in-place with `kubectl edit` results in an admission rejection; you must delete and recreate or use a new name.

question.prompt: What is the primary operational advantage of marking ConfigMaps and Secrets with `immutable: true`?

options.text: Prevents unauthorized mutations and eliminates watch overhead on the apiserver
Allows the ConfigMap to be shared across completely different clusters
Compresses the configuration data with gzip

question.explanation: Immutability protects against accidental modifications and improves apiserver scalability by stopping watch polling.

steps: Apply the ConfigMap and Secret manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-config-secrets.yaml`.
Inspect the base64-decoded Secret content: run `kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_USER}' | base64 -d`.
Verify environment variable injection in the pod: run `kubectl exec deploy/backend-worker -- env | grep -E 'DB_|LOG_'`.
Inspect the mounted configuration file: run `kubectl exec deploy/backend-worker -- cat /etc/app/config/settings.json`.

challenge.task: Create an immutable Secret containing TLS certificates and mount it as read-only files inside an NGINX pod.
acceptance: Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls` with `immutable: true`
Deployment mounting the TLS secret at `/etc/ssl/certs` in `readOnly: true` mode
CLI verification demonstrating rejection when attempting to alter the immutable secret

questions.prompt: What command generates a valid Base64 string for a Secret from the Linux command line without a trailing newline?
questions.explanation: Using `echo -n` prevents adding a trailing newline byte before passing the string to `base64`.

questions.prompt: Which directive in a Pod container spec injects all keys from a ConfigMap as individual environment variables?
questions.explanation: `envFrom` with a `configMapRef` binds all key-value entries in the ConfigMap as environment variables.

questions.prompt: What Secret type is specifically designated for storing TLS certificates and corresponding private keys?
questions.explanation: `kubernetes.io/tls` is specifically structured to require `tls.crt` and `tls.key` data keys.

questions.prompt: Why do volume-mounted ConfigMap files update inside running containers while environment variables do not?

options.text: kubelet periodically syncs mounted volume directory symlinks on the filesystem
Environment variables are deleted after pod creation
Linux kernel forbids file modifications inside containers

questions.explanation: Kubelet manages mounted volumes via atomic symlink swaps, reflecting changes on the container filesystem.

questions.prompt: How do you modify the contents of an immutable ConfigMap in a running cluster?

options.text: Delete and recreate the ConfigMap or create a new one with an incremented version name
Edit the etcd database binary directly on the control plane node

questions.explanation: Because immutable ConfigMaps reject in-place mutations, you create a new versioned ConfigMap and update the Deployment.

courses.title: 4. Services, CoreDNS & Cluster Networking
courses.summary: Master the Kubernetes IP-per-Pod network model, ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, Headless Services, CoreDNS, and EndpointSlices (CKA: Services & Networking).
courses.code:
# Kubernetes Networking: ClusterIP Service with named ports and session affinity,
# Headless Service for direct pod discovery, and backing Deployment.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-frontend-svc
  labels:
    app: web-frontend
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800
  selector:
    app: web-frontend
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db-headless-svc
  labels:
    app: db-cluster
spec:
  clusterIP: None       # Headless: CoreDNS returns A/AAAA records directly for each pod
  selector:
    app: db-cluster
  ports:
    - name: tcp-db
      port: 5432
      targetPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-frontend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-services-networking.yaml`: creates a stable ClusterIP virtual IP routing traffic to 3 backend pods on port 8080, and a Headless Service resolving direct pod IPs via CoreDNS.

lessons.title: The IP-per-Pod network model
paragraphs: Kubernetes imposes a clean, IP-per-Pod networking model with three fundamental rules: every Pod receives its own unique IP address; all Pods can communicate with all other Pods on any node without Network Address Translation (NAT); and agents on a node (such as kubelet) can communicate with all Pods on that same node.

Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins (such as Cilium with eBPF, Calico with BGP, or Flannel with VXLAN overlays) implement this specification. Because Pods are ephemeral and frequently rescheduled, their IPs change constantly, creating the need for a stable abstraction: the Kubernetes Service.
lessons.example: Pod `10.244.1.15` on Node A calls Pod `10.244.2.28` on Node B directly using its real source IP without NAT.
lessons.pitfall: Hardcoding Pod IP addresses in application configurations: Pod IPs are ephemeral and change whenever a Pod restarts or migrates.

question.prompt: What is a core requirement of the fundamental Kubernetes networking model?

options.text: Pods on different nodes must use NAT to communicate
Every Pod receives its own unique IP and communicates without NAT across nodes
All containers in a cluster must share a single IP address

question.explanation: Kubernetes requires that all Pods communicate with each other across nodes directly without address translation.

lessons.title: Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort & LoadBalancer
paragraphs: A Service provides a single, stable virtual IP (VIP) and DNS name in front of dynamic Pod endpoints. Service types define access boundaries: `ClusterIP` (default) assigns a stable IP accessible only from within the cluster; `NodePort` exposes the Service on a static high port (30000-32767) across every node's external IP.

`LoadBalancer` builds upon NodePort by automatically requesting a cloud load balancer (AWS NLB/ALB, GCP Cloud LB) or a bare-metal controller like MetalLB to route public Internet traffic into the Service. `ExternalName` maps a Service to an external CNAME DNS record without proxying.
lessons.example: ClusterIP: `10.96.0.120` (internal only). NodePort: `node-ip:31542`. LoadBalancer: `203.0.113.50` (public).
lessons.pitfall: Using `NodePort` directly in production: exposing high ports directly to the Internet bypasses central TLS termination and rate limiting.

question.prompt: Which Service type provides a stable internal IP accessible only from within the Kubernetes cluster?
question.explanation: ClusterIP is the default Service type providing an internal virtual IP reachable only from cluster workloads.

lessons.title: CoreDNS service discovery & kube-proxy
paragraphs: Kubernetes provides built-in DNS resolution via CoreDNS. When a Service is created, CoreDNS automatically generates an authoritative DNS record following the format: `<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. Pods in the same namespace can reach the Service simply by typing its short name: `curl http://web-frontend-svc`.

kube-proxy runs on each node and maintains routing rules (using iptables or IPVS modes). When a request hits a Service ClusterIP VIP, the node's packet filter intercepts the packet and transparently distributes it across healthy Pod IP endpoints using randomized or round-robin selection.
lessons.example: Cross-namespace call: `curl http://web-frontend-svc.prod-workloads.svc.cluster.local:80`.
lessons.pitfall: Believing a Service ClusterIP is a real physical network interface that answers ICMP `ping`: ClusterIPs are virtual iptables/IPVS rules, not real host interfaces.

question.prompt: What is the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for a Service named `api` in the `payments` namespace with default cluster domain?
question.explanation: The standard Kubernetes DNS FQDN is `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.

lessons.title: Headless Services & EndpointSlices
paragraphs: A Headless Service is created by explicitly specifying `clusterIP: None`. Without a ClusterIP virtual IP, kube-proxy does not create proxy rules. Instead, CoreDNS returns A/AAAA DNS records containing the individual IP addresses of all backing pods directly. This is essential for stateful systems (databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper) where clients must directly address individual cluster nodes.

Historically, the `Endpoints` resource tracked all pod IPs in a single monolithic object; large services caused massive write serialization on etcd. Modern Kubernetes uses `EndpointSlices`, breaking endpoints into scalable 100-endpoint chunks and supporting topology-aware routing to keep traffic within the same availability zone.
lessons.example: DNS query to `db-headless-svc` returns multiple A records: `10.244.1.5`, `10.244.2.9` directly to the caller.
lessons.pitfall: Creating a Headless Service when you need client-side load balancing without custom client clustering logic: the client receives a raw IP list and must handle balancing itself.

question.prompt: How do you configure a Service to be Headless so CoreDNS returns Pod IPs directly instead of a virtual VIP?
question.explanation: Setting `spec.clusterIP: None` defines a Headless Service that bypasses kube-proxy and returns Pod IPs directly in DNS.

steps: Apply the Services and Deployment: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-services-networking.yaml`.
Inspect the assigned ClusterIP and endpoints: run `kubectl get svc web-frontend-svc -o wide` and `kubectl get endpointslices`.
Perform in-cluster DNS resolution: run `kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup web-frontend-svc`.
Inspect the headless DNS records: run `kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup db-headless-svc` and verify individual pod IPs are returned.

challenge.task: Create a headless Service fronting a 3-replica StatefulSet and verify that individual pods receive dedicated DNS records matching `$(pod-name).$(service-name)`.
acceptance: Headless Service with `clusterIP: None` matching StatefulSet selector
StatefulSet declaring `serviceName` pointing to the Headless Service
Successful `nslookup` output resolving individual ordinal pod hostnames

questions.prompt: Which component is responsible for translating Service ClusterIP requests into backend Pod IP traffic using iptables or IPVS?
questions.explanation: kube-proxy manages network rules on each worker node to implement Service virtual IP routing.

questions.prompt: What default port range does Kubernetes allocate for Service objects of type NodePort?
questions.explanation: By default, NodePort allocates static ports from the 30000-32767 range across all cluster nodes.

questions.prompt: Why was EndpointSlice introduced to replace monolithic Endpoints objects in large Kubernetes clusters?

options.text: To split large endpoint sets into scalable chunks and reduce etcd write amplification
To convert TCP connections to UDP
To enforce user passwords on network connections

questions.explanation: EndpointSlices scale to thousands of endpoints by batching them into discrete slices, avoiding large monolithic updates.

questions.prompt: What field in a Service definition maps incoming traffic from the Service port to the application port inside the container?
questions.explanation: `port` is the external Service port, while `targetPort` is the port the container process listens on.

questions.prompt: If a Service selector does not match any running Pod labels, what is the observable state of its endpoints?

options.text: It forwards requests to random nodes in the cluster
The Service has zero endpoints and incoming requests immediately fail or hang
The apiserver deletes the Service automatically

questions.explanation: Without matching pod labels, the endpoint list remains empty (`<none>`), causing all traffic to drop.
