courses.title: 5. Ingress & the Gateway API
courses.summary: Master layer-7 HTTP routing, TLS termination, why Ingress is feature-frozen, and migrating to the modern Gateway API (CKA & CKAD: Services & Ingress Networking).
courses.code:
# Modern L7 Traffic Routing: Kubernetes Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1)
# with cross-service path routing, header matching, and weighted canary splitting.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: prod-gateway
  namespace: default
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy-gateway
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api-traffic-route
  namespace: default
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: prod-gateway
  hostnames:
    - "api.example.com"
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /v2
      backendRefs:
        - name: api-service-v2
          port: 8080
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
      backendRefs:
        # Weighted canary traffic splitting: 90% to stable v1, 10% to canary v2
        - name: api-service-v1
          port: 8080
          weight: 90
        - name: api-service-v2
          port: 8080
          weight: 10
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-ingress-gateway.yaml`: provisions a Gateway listener on port 80 and an HTTPRoute directing `/v2` prefix traffic to v2, while splitting root `/` traffic 90/10 between v1 and v2 services.

lessons.title: Layer 7 routing with the Ingress API
paragraphs: A Kubernetes Service operates primarily at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP). To route web traffic based on HTTP hostnames (`api.example.com` vs `store.example.com`), URL paths (`/v1` vs `/v2`), and terminate TLS at a single IP address, Kubernetes introduced the Ingress resource.

An Ingress manifest is only an abstract routing configuration; it does not route traffic by itself. It requires an Ingress Controller (such as Envoy, Traefik, or HAProxy) running in the cluster to continuously watch Ingress resources and reconfigure its underlying reverse-proxy data plane.
lessons.example: Single load balancer IP routes `example.com/api` to API service and `example.com/web` to UI service.
lessons.pitfall: Creating an Ingress manifest without an Ingress Controller installed: the Ingress object remains created in etcd but has no `ADDRESS` and routes no traffic.

question.prompt: What component must be running in the cluster for an Ingress manifest to actually route HTTP traffic?

options.text: An Ingress Controller (e.g. Envoy, Traefik, HAProxy)

question.explanation: Ingress is only a configuration spec; an active Ingress Controller is required to implement the routing proxy.

lessons.title: Why Ingress is frozen & the March 2026 milestone
paragraphs: The original Ingress API had major design flaws: it lacked expressiveness for modern L7 patterns like canary deployments, header matching, and request rewrites. To work around this, controllers relied heavily on proprietary vendor annotations (e.g. `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target`), destroying portability across cloud providers.

Crucially, the community **ingress-nginx** controller was officially **retired and archived in March 2026**, receiving no further feature releases or security patches. Consequently, the Kubernetes community has feature-frozen the Ingress API and designated the Gateway API as the official, standard successor for cloud-native traffic routing.
lessons.example: Vendor annotations that break when migrating between cloud controllers are replaced by portable Gateway API fields.
lessons.pitfall: Using legacy ingress-nginx in new 2026 production clusters: with the project retired, unpatched security vulnerabilities will not be resolved.

question.prompt: Why has the Kubernetes project feature-frozen Ingress and promoted the Gateway API as its successor?

options.text: Ingress lacked native support for advanced routing, relying on unportable annotations, and community ingress-nginx was retired in March 2026
Ingress was incompatible with Linux containers
The Gateway API requires no Kubernetes cluster to run

question.explanation: Ingress had portability issues with vendor annotations, and community ingress-nginx retired in March 2026; Gateway API is the modern GA replacement.

lessons.title: Gateway API role-oriented architecture
paragraphs: The Gateway API (`gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`, GA) solves Ingress's limitations through role-oriented separation of concerns, modeling real-world organizational boundaries: Infrastructure Providers define `GatewayClass` (specifying the underlying controller implementation); Cluster Administrators provision `Gateway` objects (defining IP addresses, ports, and TLS listeners).

Application Developers attach `HTTPRoute`, `GRPCRoute`, or `TLSRoute` objects to the Gateway. Because routes are decoupled from gateways, app developers can configure path routing, headers, and redirects independently without requiring administrative cluster privileges or risking other teams' traffic.
lessons.example: Platform team manages `Gateway` on port 443 with wildcard TLS; app teams bind their own `HTTPRoute` manifests.
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to create a Gateway without an installed GatewayClass controller (such as Envoy Gateway, Cilium, or Istio): the Gateway status remains `Programmed: False`.

question.prompt: In the Gateway API architecture, which resource do application developers author to define path and hostname routing rules?
question.explanation: Application developers author HTTPRoute resources to define routing rules and attach them to a Gateway.

lessons.title: Canary traffic splitting & header matching
paragraphs: Unlike Ingress where traffic splitting required hacky annotations, the Gateway API provides first-class support for percentage-based traffic weighting in `backendRefs`. By declaring `weight: 90` for service v1 and `weight: 10` for service v2, the gateway automatically conducts canary rollouts at Layer 7.

Gateway API routes also natively support HTTP header matching (e.g. routing requests with header `X-Beta-Tester: true` directly to experimental backends), query parameter matching, URL rewrites, and cross-namespace route attachment using `ReferenceGrant` security controls.
lessons.example: Canary rollout: `weight: 90` to v1, `weight: 10` to v2; inspect error rates before shifting 100% to v2.
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting that weights in `backendRefs` are relative to the sum of all weights: `weight: 1` and `weight: 1` yields a 50/50 split.

question.prompt: How does Gateway API implement canary traffic distribution between two backend services?

options.text: By specifying relative integer `weight` values on individual `backendRefs`
By running two identical DNS servers in the cluster
By manually shutting down pods during peak hours

question.explanation: Gateway API natively supports traffic weighting using the `weight` property in `backendRefs`.

steps: Inspect installed Gateway API CRDs: run `kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking.k8s.io`.
Apply the Gateway and HTTPRoute manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-ingress-gateway.yaml`.
Verify Gateway status: run `kubectl get gateway,httproute -o wide` to observe listener programming and assigned IP addresses.
Test canary routing: execute `curl -H 'Host: api.example.com' http://<gateway-ip>/` multiple times to verify traffic splits across backends.

challenge.task: Author an HTTPRoute that routes requests with HTTP header `X-Debug: enabled` to a debugging backend, while routing all other requests to standard production backends.
acceptance: Gateway manifest with HTTP listener on port 80
HTTPRoute using `matches.headers` with Exact type matching on `X-Debug`
Default rule forwarding unmatched traffic to standard service

questions.prompt: What major milestone occurred in March 2026 regarding the popular community ingress-nginx project?

options.text: The project was officially retired and archived, receiving no further updates
It was converted into a closed-source paid software
It was merged into Linux kernel 6.8

questions.explanation: Community ingress-nginx was retired/archived in March 2026; production clusters should adopt Gateway API.

questions.prompt: In Gateway API, what object defines cluster-wide infrastructure templates provided by the underlying controller?
questions.explanation: GatewayClass specifies the controller implementation managing Gateway instances.

questions.prompt: What path type in an HTTPRoute matches any path beginning with the specified prefix string?
questions.explanation: `PathPrefix` matches requests whose URL path starts with the configured prefix value.

questions.prompt: What security resource in Gateway API allows an HTTPRoute in one namespace to route traffic to a Service in another namespace?
questions.explanation: ReferenceGrant is the security mechanism allowing cross-namespace resource references in Gateway API.

questions.prompt: Why does Gateway API separate Gateway from HTTPRoute resources?

options.text: To separate platform operator duties from application developer routing rules
To prevent Docker from running on the master node

questions.explanation: Separating Gateway from Route objects allows platform admins to manage listeners while app teams manage routes.

courses.title: 6. Storage, PVs, PVCs & StorageClasses
courses.summary: Master persistent storage in Kubernetes: emptyDir vs hostPath, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, and CSI drivers (CKA & CKAD: Storage Architecture).
courses.code:
# Dynamic Storage Provisioning: StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer binding,
# PersistentVolumeClaim requesting 10Gi, and Deployment consuming persistent storage.
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-nvme-storage
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: database-pvc
  labels:
    tier: database
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: fast-nvme-storage
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgresql-db
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgresql-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgresql-db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16-alpine
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              value: "postgresSecurePass123!"
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5432
              name: postgres
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 512Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 1Gi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: db-persistent-storage
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
        - name: db-persistent-storage
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: database-pvc
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-storage-persistence.yaml`: StorageClass delays volume provisioning until the postgres pod is scheduled (ensuring zone alignment), binds the 10Gi PVC, and mounts it at `/var/lib/postgresql/data`.

lessons.title: Ephemeral storage vs persistent storage
paragraphs: By default, container filesystems are ephemeral: when a container crashes or is replaced, all state written to the container layer is permanently lost. Kubernetes provides temporary volumes like `emptyDir` that survive container restarts within the same Pod, but `emptyDir` data is deleted the moment the Pod itself is deleted.

`hostPath` volumes mount a directory from the worker node's host filesystem into the Pod. While data survives container restarts, `hostPath` presents severe security vulnerabilities and breaks if the Pod is rescheduled onto a different worker node. Production stateful workloads require true persistent storage.
lessons.example: `emptyDir` is fine for scratch caches; database tables require persistent volumes backed by cloud block stores or SANs.
lessons.pitfall: Using `hostPath` for production databases: when the node fails or the pod migrates, the data remains trapped on the old node.

question.prompt: What happens to data stored in an `emptyDir` volume when the Pod is deleted from the cluster?

options.text: The data is backed up to etcd automatically
The data is permanently deleted along with the Pod
The data is migrated to a new PersistentVolume

question.explanation: An emptyDir volume's lifecycle is bound directly to the Pod; deleting the Pod destroys the volume.

lessons.title: PersistentVolumes (PV) vs Claims (PVC)
paragraphs: Kubernetes cleanly separates storage management into two abstractions: PersistentVolumes (PV) and PersistentVolumeClaims (PVC). A PersistentVolume is a piece of actual storage in the cluster provisioned by an administrator or dynamically provisioned using a StorageClass. It has an independent lifecycle from any individual pod.

A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a developer's request for storage. A PVC specifies required storage capacity (e.g. `10Gi`) and access modes (e.g. `ReadWriteOnce`). The control plane reconciles PVCs by finding or provisioning a matching PV and binding them one-to-one.
lessons.example: Admin provisions 100Gi EBS volume (PV); Developer requests 10Gi (PVC); Kubernetes binds them.
lessons.pitfall: Expecting multiple PVCs to bind to the same PersistentVolume: a PV binds exclusively to one PVC in a 1-to-1 relationship.

question.prompt: What is the relationship between a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) and a PersistentVolume (PV)?

options.text: A strict 1-to-1 binding between the claim and the volume
Many PVCs can share a single PV simultaneously without restrictions
PVCs exist only in memory and never bind to PVs

question.explanation: Binding between a PVC and a PV is a mutually exclusive 1-to-1 mapping.

lessons.title: StorageClasses & volume binding modes
paragraphs: In modern clusters, manual PV provisioning does not scale. A `StorageClass` enables dynamic volume provisioning: when a user creates a PVC referencing a StorageClass, the underlying Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver automatically communicates with the cloud provider or SAN API to provision the disk on demand.

StorageClasses define `volumeBindingMode`: `Immediate` provisions the volume immediately when the PVC is created; `WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until a Pod requesting the PVC is scheduled. `WaitForFirstConsumer` is critical in multi-zone clusters to ensure the volume is created in the exact availability zone where the Pod is scheduled.
lessons.example: With `WaitForFirstConsumer`, AWS EBS creates the volume in `us-east-1a` because the Pod was placed on a node in `us-east-1a`.
lessons.pitfall: Using `volumeBindingMode: Immediate` in multi-AZ clusters: the volume might be provisioned in zone `us-east-1a` while the pod gets scheduled in `us-east-1b`, rendering the disk unattachable.

question.prompt: Why is `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` strongly recommended for cloud block storage in multi-AZ clusters?

options.text: It guarantees the volume is provisioned in the same availability zone as the scheduled Pod
It compresses the volume size by 80%
It allows block storage to be mounted by unlimited pods across all nodes

question.explanation: WaitForFirstConsumer delays disk provisioning until pod scheduling is decided, preventing cross-zone attachment failures.

lessons.title: Access modes & volume expansion
paragraphs: Kubernetes storage volumes support four distinct access modes: `ReadWriteOnce` (RWO - mountable as read-write by a single node), `ReadOnlyMany` (ROX - mountable read-only by many nodes), `ReadWriteMany` (RWX - mountable read-write by many nodes simultaneously, typical for NFS or CephFS), and `ReadWriteOncePod` (RWOP - accessible by a single pod).

When disk space runs low, setting `allowVolumeExpansion: true` on the StorageClass permits dynamic volume expansion. Administrators edit the PVC's `spec.resources.requests.storage` to a larger size (e.g. from `10Gi` to `20Gi`), and the CSI driver automatically expands the underlying filesystem online without unmounting the disk.
lessons.example: Standard block storage (AWS EBS, GCP PD) supports `ReadWriteOnce`; shared filesystems (NFS, AWS EFS) support `ReadWriteMany`.
lessons.pitfall: Attempting to mount a `ReadWriteOnce` block volume simultaneously on two pods running on two different worker nodes: the cloud provider will reject the second attachment.

question.prompt: Which volume access mode allows multiple worker nodes to mount the volume simultaneously for read-write access?
question.explanation: ReadWriteMany (RWX) allows concurrent read-write mounts across multiple cluster nodes (e.g. NFS).

steps: Inspect cluster StorageClasses: run `kubectl get storageclass` to see default provisioners.
Apply the storage manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-storage-persistence.yaml`.
Observe PVC status change: run `kubectl get pvc,pv` to observe the PVC transition from `Pending` to `Bound` once the pod schedules.
Test online volume expansion: run `kubectl patch pvc database-pvc -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"15Gi"}}}}'`.

challenge.task: Configure a StorageClass with `allowVolumeExpansion: true` and demonstrate expanding an active PVC from 5Gi to 10Gi without deleting the pod.
acceptance: StorageClass manifest with dynamic CSI provisioner and volume expansion enabled
PVC initially bound at 5Gi and successfully expanded to 10Gi
`kubectl describe pvc` output showing successful file system resizing

questions.prompt: What component in Kubernetes standardizes the interface between storage vendors and container orchestrators?
questions.explanation: CSI is the specification for developing out-of-tree storage plugins for Kubernetes.

questions.prompt: What reclaim policy retains the underlying PersistentVolume when its associated PVC is deleted, allowing manual data recovery?
questions.explanation: The `Retain` reclaim policy preserves the PV and its underlying storage after PVC deletion.

questions.prompt: What access mode restricts volume access to exactly one Pod, preventing even other Pods on the same node from mounting it?
questions.explanation: ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) restricts access to a single pod in the entire cluster.

questions.prompt: Which field in a StorageClass must be enabled before you can increase the size of an existing PVC?
questions.explanation: Volume expansion requires `allowVolumeExpansion: true` in the StorageClass definition.

questions.prompt: Why is `hostPath` storage considered insecure and fragile for production workloads?

options.text: It gives pods direct access to the host filesystem and breaks if the pod migrates to another node
It can only store up to 1 megabyte of data
It requires the host to run Windows

questions.explanation: hostPath binds workloads to specific node filesystems, creating security risks and preventing migration.

courses.title: 7. StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs & CronJobs
courses.summary: Master stateful and batch workloads: stable network identities, volumeClaimTemplates, node-wide DaemonSets, batch Jobs, and CronJobs (CKAD: Multi-container & Batch Workloads).
courses.code:
# Stateful and Batch Workloads: StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates,
# Headless Service, and an automated database backup CronJob.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis-headless
  labels:
    app: redis-cluster
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: redis-cluster
  ports:
    - port: 6379
      name: redis
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: redis-node
spec:
  serviceName: redis-headless
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis-cluster
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis-cluster
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: redis
          image: redis:7.2-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
              name: redis
          volumeMounts:
            - name: redis-data
              mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: redis-data
      spec:
        accessModes: [ "ReadWriteOnce" ]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 5Gi
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: redis-backup-job
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"         # Daily at 02:00 UTC
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid     # Prevent overlapping backup executions
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 2
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: backup-runner
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo "Starting Redis backup snapshot..."; sleep 3; echo "Backup successfully stored to S3 bucket."']
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-statefulsets-daemonsets.yaml`: provisions 3 stateful Redis pods named `redis-node-0`, `redis-node-1`, `redis-node-2` with dedicated 5Gi PVCs, and registers a daily automated backup CronJob.

lessons.title: StatefulSets & stable network identity
paragraphs: Unlike Deployments where Pods are interchangeable and assigned random hashes (e.g. `web-7d9f6b-xk92m`), a StatefulSet manages stateful applications requiring unique, persistent identities. Pods in a StatefulSet are assigned a fixed ordinal index (0, 1, 2, ...): `redis-node-0`, `redis-node-1`, `redis-node-2`.

Paired with a Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`), each Pod receives a deterministic, predictable DNS hostname formatted as `$(pod-name).$(service-name)` (e.g. `redis-node-0.redis-headless`). StatefulSets perform ordered sequential startups (0 must become ready before 1 launches) and ordered terminations (2 terminates before 1).
lessons.example: Primary node `redis-node-0` initializes first; replicas `redis-node-1` and `redis-node-2` replicate from `redis-node-0.redis-headless`.
lessons.pitfall: Using a standard Deployment for clustering software like ZooKeeper, Cassandra, or etcd: without ordinal identity and stable DNS, cluster peers cannot reliably discover each other.

question.prompt: What naming format does a StatefulSet assign to its Pods?

options.text: Fixed ordinal indexes starting at 0 (e.g. redis-node-0, redis-node-1)
The MAC address of the worker node

question.explanation: StatefulSet pods receive stable, predictable ordinal names (0, 1, 2) that remain constant across restarts.

lessons.title: volumeClaimTemplates & persistent state
paragraphs: In a Deployment, all pod replicas mount the exact same PVC if configured, causing write conflicts unless using shared filesystems. In contrast, a StatefulSet defines `volumeClaimTemplates`. When the StatefulSet scales up, Kubernetes automatically creates a dedicated, distinct PVC for each individual pod replica (e.g. `redis-data-redis-node-0`, `redis-data-redis-node-1`).

When a StatefulSet pod crashes or is rescheduled to a different node, Kubernetes guarantees that the replacement pod with ordinal 0 reattaches to the exact same PVC (`redis-data-redis-node-0`). Crucially, scaling down a StatefulSet does NOT delete the PVCs, safeguarding data against accidental scale-down events.
lessons.example: Scaling down from 3 to 2 preserves `redis-data-redis-node-2`; scaling back up to 3 reattaches the existing disk.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming deleting a StatefulSet deletes its PVCs: PVCs created by `volumeClaimTemplates` are never automatically deleted; they must be removed manually.

question.prompt: What happens to the PVCs created by a StatefulSet's `volumeClaimTemplates` when the StatefulSet is scaled down or deleted?

options.text: They are immediately formatted and erased
They are retained intact to prevent accidental data loss

question.explanation: Kubernetes retains volumeClaimTemplate PVCs to prevent accidental data loss when scaling down or deleting StatefulSets.

lessons.title: DaemonSets for node-wide infrastructure
paragraphs: A DaemonSet ensures that all (or some subset of) nodes run a single copy of a Pod. As new nodes join the cluster, the DaemonSet controller automatically schedules a pod onto them; as nodes leave or are terminated, those pods are garbage collected.

DaemonSets are the standard pattern for running node-level infrastructure services: log collectors (Fluentbit, Promtail), host metrics monitors (Prometheus Node Exporter), storage daemons (Ceph CSI), and network overlay daemons (Cilium, Calico). DaemonSets often include tolerations allowing them to run on control plane nodes.
lessons.example: `node-exporter` DaemonSet runs exactly 1 pod per node to expose CPU, memory, and disk I/O metrics to Prometheus.
lessons.pitfall: Using Deployments for cluster log collectors: a Deployment might schedule 4 log pods on 1 node and 0 pods on 3 other nodes, leaving those nodes unmonitored.

question.prompt: Which workload controller guarantees that exactly one copy of a Pod runs on every worker node in the cluster?
question.explanation: DaemonSets ensure that all eligible nodes run exactly one replica of the specified Pod.

lessons.title: Batch processing with Jobs & CronJobs
paragraphs: While Deployments and StatefulSets run continuous, long-running services (where containers are expected to never exit), a Kubernetes `Job` runs a batch process to successful completion (exit code 0). Jobs specify `completions` (total required successful runs), `parallelism` (concurrent pods), and `backoffLimit` (retry attempts before failing).

A `CronJob` executes Jobs on a time-based schedule using standard cron syntax (`min hour day month day-of-week`). CronJobs configure `concurrencyPolicy`: `Allow` (permits overlapping executions), `Forbid` (skips the new run if the previous job is still running), and `Replace` (cancels the currently running job and starts a new one).
lessons.example: Daily backup CronJob with `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` ensures two backup processes never run simultaneously.
lessons.pitfall: Using `concurrencyPolicy: Allow` for resource-heavy batch jobs: if a job hangs, new runs trigger repeatedly until node memory is exhausted.

question.prompt: Which `concurrencyPolicy` setting on a CronJob prevents a new scheduled job from starting if the previous execution is still running?
question.explanation: `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` skips starting a new job instance if the currently running job has not completed.

steps: Apply the StatefulSet and CronJob: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-statefulsets-daemonsets.yaml`.
Observe ordered pod startup: run `kubectl get pods -l app=redis-cluster -w` and notice `redis-node-0` reaches Ready before `redis-node-1` begins creation.
Verify dedicated PVC creation: run `kubectl get pvc -l app=redis-cluster` to observe the three unique volumeClaimTemplate PVCs.
Manually trigger the CronJob to create a Job: run `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/redis-backup-job manual-backup-1` and check logs with `kubectl logs job/manual-backup-1`.

challenge.task: Deploy a 3-node StatefulSet, write unique data into ordinal 0, delete pod 0, and verify the replacement pod mounts the identical PVC and preserves data.
acceptance: StatefulSet with headless service and volumeClaimTemplates
Writing a unique file into `/data` on pod ordinal 0
Deleting pod 0 with `kubectl delete pod` and verifying file contents on the restarted pod

questions.prompt: What happens when you delete a StatefulSet in Kubernetes regarding its persistent volume claims?

options.text: The associated PVCs are automatically deleted immediately
The associated PVCs remain intact and are not deleted

questions.explanation: PVCs created by StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates are retained to prevent accidental data destruction.

questions.prompt: What type of Service must be referenced in a StatefulSet's `serviceName` field to enable direct pod DNS resolution?
questions.explanation: StatefulSets require a Headless Service to provide individual DNS records for each ordinal pod.

questions.prompt: What pod restartPolicy is valid inside a batch Job pod template?
questions.explanation: Job containers must terminate upon completion, so restartPolicy must be OnFailure or Never (not Always).

questions.prompt: What controller is best suited for running Prometheus Node Exporter across every node in the cluster?
questions.explanation: DaemonSets ensure host monitoring agents run exactly once on every physical/virtual worker node.

questions.prompt: What happens if a CronJob schedule triggers while a previous job is still running under `concurrencyPolicy: Replace`?

options.text: The currently running job is cancelled and terminated, and the new job starts

questions.explanation: The `Replace` concurrency policy terminates the active running job and replaces it with the new job.

courses.title: 8. Scheduling, Health Probes & Resource Management
courses.summary: Master advanced scheduling, node affinity, taints and tolerations, container health probes (startup/liveness/readiness), QoS classes, and OOM prevention (CKA: Scheduling & Maintenance).
courses.code:
# Resilient Workload: Pod anti-affinity across failure domains, tolerations,
# startup/liveness/readiness probes, and Guaranteed Quality of Service (QoS).
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: resilient-api
  labels:
    app: resilient-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resilient-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: resilient-api
    spec:
      affinity:
        # Anti-affinity: Spread replicas across different physical nodes
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 100
              podAffinityTerm:
                labelSelector:
                  matchExpressions:
                    - key: app
                      operator: In
                      values:
                        - resilient-api
                topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      tolerations:
        - key: "workload-type"
          operator: "Equal"
          value: "compute-heavy"
          effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
        - name: web-api
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
              name: http
          resources:
            # Equal requests and limits guarantee Guaranteed QoS class
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 12   # Up to 60s for initialization
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
            timeoutSeconds: 2
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-scheduling-resilience.yaml`: places replicas across distinct nodes using pod anti-affinity, assigns Guaranteed QoS class, protects slow bootups with startupProbe, and isolates traffic until readiness passes.

lessons.title: Scheduler internals: Filtering and scoring
paragraphs: When a Pod is submitted without a `nodeName`, the kube-scheduler assigns it to an eligible node through a two-phase process: Filtering (predicates) and Scoring (priorities). In the Filtering phase, the scheduler eliminates nodes that cannot run the Pod (e.g. insufficient CPU/memory, port conflicts, unmet taints, or missing node labels).

In the Scoring phase, the scheduler ranks the surviving candidate nodes using priority plugins (such as ImageLocality, NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation, and Affinity weights). The node with the highest combined score is chosen, and a `Binding` object is written to the apiserver, notifying the node's kubelet to start the containers.
lessons.example: 10-node cluster -> Filtering finds 4 nodes with available memory -> Scoring ranks them -> Node 3 selected.
lessons.pitfall: Setting hard node constraints (`nodeName`) in manifests: hardcoded node binding bypasses scheduler logic and causes pod scheduling failure if that specific node goes offline.

question.prompt: What are the two sequential phases executed by kube-scheduler to select a node for an unscheduled Pod?

options.text: Filtering (eliminates ineligible nodes) and Scoring (ranks candidate nodes)

question.explanation: Kube-scheduler first filters out nodes that cannot satisfy pod requirements, then scores remaining nodes to pick the best match.

lessons.title: Node affinity & pod anti-affinity
paragraphs: Node affinity allows you to constrain which nodes your Pod can be scheduled on based on node labels. It supports two rules: `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` (hard requirement: the Pod will not be scheduled unless a matching node exists) and `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` (soft preference: the scheduler will try to match, but will schedule elsewhere if necessary).

Pod anti-affinity prevents co-locating Pod replicas of the same service on the same failure domain. By setting `topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname` or `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, Kubernetes ensures that replicas are spread across different physical servers or cloud availability zones, preventing a single hardware failure from taking down your entire service.
lessons.example: Pod anti-affinity across availability zones ensures 1 zone outage leaves 66% of application replicas running.
lessons.pitfall: Using hard `requiredDuringScheduling` pod anti-affinity with 5 replicas on a 3-node cluster: 2 pods will remain stuck in `Pending` forever because nodes are exhausted.

question.prompt: Which pod anti-affinity rule should you use if you want to spread replicas across nodes when possible, but allow co-location if the cluster runs out of nodes?
question.explanation: Preferred rules express soft affinity preferences, allowing pods to schedule even if co-location cannot be avoided.

lessons.title: Taints, tolerations & node draining
paragraphs: Node affinity attracts Pods to nodes; conversely, Taints allow a node to repel a set of Pods. A taint has the format `key=value:effect`, with three effects: `NoSchedule` (new non-tolerating pods cannot schedule), `PreferNoSchedule` (soft avoid), and `NoExecute` (immediately evicts existing non-tolerating pods).

Tolerations are declared in the PodSpec, permitting (but not requiring) the Pod to schedule onto matching tainted nodes. When performing node maintenance, running `kubectl drain <node>` applies a `NoSchedule` taint, cordons the node, and gracefully evicts all running pods to other nodes without application downtime.
lessons.example: GPU nodes have taint `gpu=true:NoSchedule`; only ML training pods declaring `tolerations: [{key: 'gpu', value: 'true'}]` can schedule there.
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting that tolerating a taint does not guarantee placement on that node: you must combine tolerations with nodeSelector or nodeAffinity to ensure exclusive placement.

question.prompt: What taint effect immediately evicts non-tolerating pods currently running on the node?
question.explanation: `NoExecute` evicts any existing running pods that do not have a matching toleration.

lessons.title: Health probes, QoS classes & OOMKilled
paragraphs: Kubernetes provides three distinct health probes: `startupProbe` (checks if legacy/slow apps have finished initialization, pausing other probes), `livenessProbe` (detects application deadlocks; if it fails, kubelet restarts the container), and `readinessProbe` (determines if the container is ready to accept traffic; if it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints without restarting).

Kubernetes categorizes Pods into three Quality of Service (QoS) classes: `Guaranteed` (CPU and Memory limits match requests exactly), `Burstable` (requests are set but lower than limits), and `BestEffort` (no requests or limits set). When node memory is exhausted, the Linux kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminates BestEffort pods first, then Burstable, preserving Guaranteed pods until the very end.
lessons.example: If memory limit is 256Mi and app consumes 257Mi, the container is immediately killed with `Exit Code 137 (OOMKilled)`.
lessons.pitfall: Using a livenessProbe that calls external dependencies (e.g. database): if the database goes down, the livenessProbe fails and kubelet restarts all application pods in a cascading crash loop.

question.prompt: Which health probe removes a Pod from Service load balancer endpoints when failing, without restarting the container?
question.explanation: readinessProbe governs traffic admission; failing readiness removes the pod from endpoints while allowing the container to continue running.

steps: Apply the resilient workload manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-scheduling-resilience.yaml`.
Verify the assigned QoS class: run `kubectl get pod -l app=resilient-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.qosClass}'` and verify it displays `Guaranteed`.
Simulate readiness failure: run `kubectl exec deploy/resilient-api -- rm -f /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html` and observe `kubectl get endpoints` removing the unready pod.
Inspect pod anti-affinity distribution: run `kubectl get pods -l app=resilient-api -o wide` to verify replicas are placed on different worker nodes.

challenge.task: Taint a worker node with `dedicated=ml-gpu:NoSchedule`, configure a deployment with a matching toleration and nodeSelector, and verify scheduling.
acceptance: Node tainted with `kubectl taint nodes <node-name> dedicated=ml-gpu:NoSchedule`
Deployment manifest specifying matching toleration and nodeAffinity
Verification that pods schedule exclusively on the tainted node

questions.prompt: What exit code indicates that a container was terminated by the Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer for exceeding its memory limit?
questions.explanation: Exit Code 137 indicates process termination by SIGKILL (9) due to exceeding memory limits (OOMKilled).

questions.prompt: What Quality of Service (QoS) class is assigned to a Pod where CPU and Memory requests and limits are explicitly set and equal for all containers?
questions.explanation: A Pod achieves Guaranteed QoS when every container specifies requests and limits that are identical for both CPU and memory.

questions.prompt: What probe should be used to protect a Java application that takes 45 seconds to initialize its JVM and load caches?
questions.explanation: startupProbe disables liveness and readiness checks until the application has completed its initial slow bootup.

questions.prompt: What command safely evicts all workloads from a node prior to rebooting or conducting hardware maintenance?
questions.explanation: `kubectl drain` cordons the node and evicts running pods respecting PodDisruptionBudgets.

questions.prompt: Why should liveness probes NEVER execute checks against external dependencies like a backend database or external API?

options.text: If the external dependency fails, all application instances will fail liveness and restart simultaneously in a cascading outage
Kubernetes forbids outbound network calls during probes
Database drivers do not work inside containers

questions.explanation: Liveness probes must only check local container health; testing external dependencies causes catastrophic cascading restart storms.

courses.title: 9. Security: RBAC, NetworkPolicies & Pod Hardening
courses.summary: Master cluster security: least-privilege RBAC, workload ServiceAccounts, default-deny NetworkPolicies, Pod Security Standards, and container hardening (CKS & CKA: Cluster Security & Hardening).
courses.code:
# Production Security Hardening: Least-privilege RBAC, default-deny NetworkPolicy,
# and restricted securityContext with dropped capabilities and non-root user.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: secured-api-sa
  namespace: default
automountServiceAccountToken: false  # Disable projected token when API access is unneeded
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: config-reader-role
  namespace: default
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: bind-config-reader
  namespace: default
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: secured-api-sa
    namespace: default
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: config-reader-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-and-allow-ingress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secured-workload
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
  ingress:
    # Allow ingress on port 8080 only from frontend pods
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              tier: frontend
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
  egress:
    # Allow egress only to CoreDNS for name resolution
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: {}
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secured-workload
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secured-workload
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: secured-workload
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: secured-api-sa
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        runAsGroup: 10001
        fsGroup: 10001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop:
                - ALL
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tmp-scratch
              mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
        - name: tmp-scratch
          emptyDir: {}
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-security-rbac.yaml`: grants read-only configmap permissions to `secured-api-sa`, enforces default-deny NetworkPolicy, drops all Linux capabilities, and runs container as non-root with read-only rootfs.

lessons.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
paragraphs: Kubernetes RBAC regulates access to the apiserver REST resources based on the principle of least privilege. An RBAC rule combines three elements: `apiGroups` (e.g. `""` for core, `apps`, `batch`), `resources` (e.g. `pods`, `services`, `secrets`), and `verbs` (e.g. `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `delete`).

`Role` and `RoleBinding` are namespace-scoped, restricting permissions to a single namespace. `ClusterRole` and `ClusterRoleBinding` apply cluster-wide across all namespaces (or to cluster-scoped resources like nodes and namespaces). Avoid wildcards (`*`) in production roles, as granting `create pods` or wildcard verbs allows privilege escalation to cluster-admin.
lessons.example: Read-only config role grants `verbs: ["get", "list"]` on `resources: ["configmaps"]` in namespace `prod`.
lessons.pitfall: Granting `*` verbs on `*` resources in a ClusterRoleBinding: this gives full root cluster-admin access to the subject.

question.prompt: What is the scope difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?

options.text: Role is confined to a specific namespace; ClusterRole applies cluster-wide
Role is for containers; ClusterRole is for virtual machines
Role requires Python; ClusterRole requires Go

question.explanation: Roles bind permissions within a specific namespace, whereas ClusterRoles define permissions cluster-wide.

lessons.title: Workload identity with ServiceAccounts
paragraphs: While human users authenticate via external Identity Providers (OIDC, LDAP), in-cluster applications authenticate to the kube-apiserver using `ServiceAccounts`. By default, Kubernetes mounts a projected ServiceAccount JSON Web Token (JWT) into every pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount`.

If your application workload does not communicate with the Kubernetes API, you should explicitly set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount or PodSpec. In cloud environments (AWS EKS IRSA, GCP Workload Identity), ServiceAccounts integrate directly with IAM roles, eliminating the need to store static AWS or GCP keys in the cluster.
lessons.example: Setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` prevents an attacker who exploits an app RCE from stealing the API token.
lessons.pitfall: Leaving `default` ServiceAccounts with unneeded cluster-admin privileges: any compromised container in that namespace can take over the cluster.

question.prompt: Why should `automountServiceAccountToken: false` be set on Pods that do not talk to the Kubernetes API?

options.text: To prevent an attacker who compromises the container from reading the API token and accessing the cluster
Because mounting tokens slows down CPU speed by 20%
To allow the container to run without an operating system

question.explanation: Disabling token automounting adheres to least privilege and stops attackers from hijacking cluster API tokens.

lessons.title: NetworkPolicies & microsegmentation
paragraphs: By default, the Kubernetes network is completely open: any Pod can establish TCP/UDP connections to any other Pod across any namespace. A `NetworkPolicy` acts as a distributed Layer 3/Layer 4 packet firewall enforced by the CNI plugin (e.g. Cilium or Calico) at each node's virtual interface.

Production clusters enforce a Default-Deny posture: once a NetworkPolicy selects a Pod with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]`, all incoming and outgoing connections are blocked unless explicitly whitelisted by `from` or `to` rules matching specific `podSelector`, `namespaceSelector`, or `ipBlock` CIDRs.
lessons.example: Default-deny policy blocks all traffic to the database pod except incoming traffic from pods labelled `app: backend` on port 5432.
lessons.pitfall: Applying NetworkPolicies in clusters running Flannel without an active network policy provider: Flannel does not enforce NetworkPolicies, leaving traffic completely open.

question.prompt: What is the default network communication behavior between two Pods in different namespaces if no NetworkPolicies exist?

options.text: All communication is completely allowed by default

question.explanation: In standard Kubernetes, network traffic between all pods across all namespaces is unrestricted by default.

lessons.title: Pod Security Standards & securityContext
paragraphs: The Pod Security Standards (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted) define cluster-wide hardening tiers enforced via namespace labels (e.g. `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`). Workloads under the Restricted profile must run without root privileges and with hardened Linux kernel isolation.

Container hardening is configured in `securityContext`: `runAsNonRoot: true` (refuses to start images running as UID 0/root), `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` (prevents attackers from writing binaries or malicious scripts to `/bin` or `/usr`), `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` (blocks setuid binaries), and `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` (strips all Linux kernel capabilities like NET_ADMIN and SYS_ADMIN).
lessons.example: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` forces temporary writes into an explicit emptyDir at `/tmp`, blocking malware persistence.
lessons.pitfall: Running containers as root (UID 0): if a container breakout vulnerability exists in the runtime, the attacker immediately gains root access to the host node.

question.prompt: Which `securityContext` setting prevents processes inside a container from writing or modifying files on the container root filesystem?
question.explanation: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` mounts the root container layer as read-only, preventing malicious filesystem tampering.

steps: Test RBAC permissions: run `kubectl auth can-i list configmaps --as=system:serviceaccount:default:secured-api-sa`.
Apply the security manifest: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-security-rbac.yaml`.
Verify container non-root UID: run `kubectl exec deploy/secured-workload -- id` and verify it displays `uid=10001`.
Verify read-only filesystem: run `kubectl exec deploy/secured-workload -- touch /test.txt` and observe rejection with `Read-only file system`.

challenge.task: Configure a namespace with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` and deploy a fully hardened microservice adhering to Restricted standards.
acceptance: Namespace labelled with Pod Security Standard `restricted` enforcement
Deployment with `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, and `capabilities.drop: [ALL]`
Successful admission and running status under Restricted policy

questions.prompt: What CLI command allows you to verify whether a specific user or ServiceAccount has permission to execute an action?
questions.explanation: `kubectl auth can-i` checks the apiserver authorization engine to determine if an action is permitted.

questions.prompt: What capability setting ensures that no Linux capabilities are retained by the container process?
questions.explanation: Specifying `drop: ["ALL"]` under capabilities strips all default Linux kernel capabilities from the container.

questions.prompt: What happens if a pod runs in a namespace labelled with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` and sets `privileged: true`?

options.text: The apiserver admission controller rejects the Pod creation with a validation error

questions.explanation: Pod Security Standards admission rejects pods that violate the enforced security level.

questions.prompt: What seccomp profile type should be configured in `securityContext` to apply the container runtime's default system call filter?
questions.explanation: `seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }` enables the runtime's default seccomp syscall filter.

questions.prompt: Which NetworkPolicy specification enables a default-deny rule for all incoming traffic to selected pods?

options.text: policyTypes: [Ingress] with empty ingress rules list

questions.explanation: Selecting `policyTypes: [Ingress]` without defining any matching `ingress` rules enforces an ingress default-deny.

# Production Capstone: Zero-downtime microservice architecture featuring Namespace,
# PodDisruptionBudget (PDB), Deployment with probes/resources, Service,
# HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA v2), and isolated NetworkPolicy.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: enterprise-app
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: microservice-pdb
  namespace: enterprise-app
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: enterprise-service
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: enterprise-service
  namespace: enterprise-app
  labels:
    app: enterprise-service
spec:
  replicas: 2
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: enterprise-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: enterprise-service
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: server
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop:
                - ALL
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: enterprise-service
  namespace: enterprise-app
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: enterprise-service
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: enterprise-service-hpa
  namespace: enterprise-app
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: enterprise-service
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 80
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 20
          periodSeconds: 60
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: enterprise-isolation
  namespace: enterprise-app
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: enterprise-service
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
courses.expected: Applied with `kubectl apply -f k8s-capstone.yaml`: creates the restricted namespace, protects availability with PDB (minAvailable: 2), deploys the hardened microservice, exposes ClusterIP service, scales automatically from 2 to 10 pods via HPA v2, and restricts ingress traffic.

lessons.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA v2) & Karpenter
paragraphs: Kubernetes provides autoscaling across two dimensions: workload pod autoscaling and node cluster autoscaling. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA v2) queries the metrics API (powered by `metrics-server` or custom Prometheus adapters) and automatically scales Deployment replicas up or down based on observed CPU utilization, memory pressure, or custom application metrics (e.g. SQS queue depth, HTTP requests/sec).

HPA v2 includes configurable scaling `behavior`: scaling up aggressively during traffic surges while dampening scale-downs with a `stabilizationWindowSeconds` (e.g. 300 seconds) to prevent flapping. When pods cannot schedule because worker nodes are full, cluster autoscalers or modern just-in-time node provisioners like Karpenter provision new cloud compute instances in seconds.
lessons.example: Traffic spikes -> CPU reaches 85% (>70% target) -> HPA scales replicas from 2 to 6 -> Load normalizes.
lessons.pitfall: Configuring HPA on a Deployment without specifying container resource `requests`: without explicit requests, the metrics server cannot calculate percentage utilization and HPA fails.

question.prompt: What container specification is strictly mandatory for the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to compute target percentage utilization?

options.text: Container resource `requests` for the targeted metric

question.explanation: HPA computes percentage utilization against resource requests (`actual_usage / requested * 100`).

lessons.title: Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) & Operators
paragraphs: The true superpower of Kubernetes is its extensibility. A Custom Resource Definition (CRD) extends the Kubernetes API by introducing new declarative resource types (e.g. `PostgreSQLCluster`, `CertManagerCertificate`, `ArgoWorkflow`) registered dynamically with the kube-apiserver without modifying core Kubernetes source code.

The Operator Pattern combines a CRD with a custom reconciliation controller (typically written in Go, Rust, or Python with Kopf). The Operator codifies domain-specific operational human knowledge: managing automated database backups, automated cluster failover, rolling schema upgrades, and self-healing distributed systems.
lessons.example: A Prometheus Operator watches `ServiceMonitor` CRDs and automatically reconfigures Prometheus scrape targets.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming creating a CRD makes it functional: a CRD only stores state in etcd; an active controller must be running to reconcile and actuate the custom resource.

question.prompt: What two components form the core of the Kubernetes Operator Pattern?

options.text: A Custom Resource Definition (CRD) and a custom reconciliation controller
Docker Compose and a Bash script
A hardware RAID controller and a SAN

question.explanation: The Operator pattern pairs custom declarative schemas (CRDs) with an active controller reconciliation loop.

lessons.title: Helm package manager & templating
paragraphs: Managing dozens of static raw YAML manifests across multiple environments (dev, staging, prod) leads to duplication and errors. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. Helm packages manifests into reusable units called Charts containing three core components: `Chart.yaml` (metadata), `values.yaml` (default configuration values), and `templates/` (Go-templated Kubernetes manifests).

Helm renders templates dynamically by combining manifests with environment-specific values files (`helm install my-app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml`). Helm tracks release revisions in cluster Secrets, enabling one-command upgrades (`helm upgrade`) and atomic rollbacks (`helm rollback`).
lessons.example: Deploy a complete multi-replica Redis cluster with persistence in one command: `helm install my-redis bitnami/redis`.
lessons.pitfall: Editing Helm-managed Kubernetes resources directly with `kubectl edit`: the changes will be overwritten on the next `helm upgrade`.

question.prompt: Which file in a Helm chart provides the default configurable parameters that are injected into manifest templates?
question.explanation: `values.yaml` defines default parameters that can be overridden during installation or upgrades.

lessons.title: GitOps delivery & PodDisruptionBudgets
paragraphs: GitOps is the operational framework where Git is the single source of truth for all declarative cluster infrastructure and application state. Tools like ArgoCD or Flux run inside the cluster, continuously comparing the desired state in Git against the live cluster state, automatically deploying changes and correcting manual cluster drift.

To guarantee zero-downtime during cluster maintenance (such as node upgrades or `kubectl drain`), applications declare a `PodDisruptionBudget` (PDB). A PDB specifies `minAvailable` (e.g. `2`) or `maxUnavailable` (e.g. `10%`). When an administrative node drain occurs, the eviction API blocks node evictions until replacement pods are running elsewhere, preventing outages.
lessons.example: Git commit pushed to `main` branch -> ArgoCD detects diff -> ArgoCD syncs cluster state declaratively.
lessons.pitfall: Configuring a PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 2` on a Deployment with only 1 replica: `kubectl drain` will hang indefinitely because the PDB cannot be satisfied.

question.prompt: What is the purpose of a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) during voluntary cluster operations like node drains?

options.text: It guarantees that a minimum number or percentage of healthy replicas remain available during voluntary disruptions
It limits the monthly dollar cost of the cloud bill
It automatically purchases new physical servers

question.explanation: PDBs protect application availability by limiting the number of pods that can be voluntarily evicted at the same time.

steps: Apply the complete production capstone: run `kubectl apply -f k8s-capstone.yaml`.
Verify the PodDisruptionBudget: run `kubectl get pdb -n enterprise-app` and verify `MIN AVAILABLE` is 2.
Inspect the active HPA status: run `kubectl get hpa -n enterprise-app` to observe current CPU and memory utilization against targets.

Simulate traffic load to trigger horizontal autoscaling: run `kubectl run load-generator --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- /bin/sh -c 'while true; do wget -q -O- http://enterprise-service.enterprise-app; done'` and watch replicas scale up with `kubectl get hpa -n enterprise-app -w`.

acceptance: Helm chart templating a hardened Deployment, Service, PDB, and HPA v2
Demonstration of HPA scaling from 2 to 5 replicas during load testing
Execution of `kubectl drain` with zero dropped requests verified by PDB protection

questions.prompt: What core tenet defines the GitOps operational methodology?

options.text: Git is the sole declarative source of truth, and automated in-cluster controllers reconcile drift
Developers deploy directly to production using imperative SSH commands
Kubernetes clusters must run without any network connectivity

questions.explanation: GitOps uses Git as the authoritative source of truth, with pull-based agents reconciling cluster state.

questions.prompt: In HPA v2, what parameter prevents rapid fluctuating scale-down actions (thrashing/flapping) following temporary traffic spikes?
questions.explanation: The stabilization window ensures that historical peak metrics are evaluated before scaling down, preventing thrashing.

questions.prompt: What happens if a node drain command (`kubectl drain`) attempts to evict a pod, but doing so would violate the pod's PodDisruptionBudget?

options.text: The eviction API temporarily blocks and waits until replacement pods are healthy
The node is immediately powered off

questions.explanation: The eviction API honors PDB constraints and blocks evictions that would violate minimum availability thresholds.

questions.prompt: What command allows you to roll back a Helm release to a previous revision number?
questions.explanation: `helm rollback` reverts the Helm release to the specified historical revision.

questions.prompt: How does an Operator extend Kubernetes capabilities beyond built-in controllers?

options.text: It combines Custom Resource Definitions with custom controllers to automate domain-specific operational tasks
It modifies the Linux kernel source code on worker nodes
It replaces kube-apiserver with an Apache web server

questions.explanation: Operators encapsulate domain-specific operational expertise (backups, failover, upgrades) using CRDs and custom controllers.
